editorial.headline: Online Game Publishing: Nationally Open, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Online game software publishing is open to full foreign ownership nationally, but in Bali the PMA route turns on the exact scope’s OSS risk classification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 58211 is for publishing online video-game software ready to operate across operating-system platforms and devices. It includes a publisher’s provision of online games to every type of user, including subscribers, and expressly encompasses in-game and in-app purchases. It also covers intermediation services connected to the publishing of online game software. The unifying activity is the online publication and provision of a game across the platforms and users named in the scope.

The activity is not confined to one business size. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, giving the category a broad formal scale range. Across that range, the stated activity remains online game publishing, game provision by the publisher, and the defined intermediation services. The scope is expansive in its platform and user reach, yet specific in its focus on online video-game software publishing.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity carries TERBUKA status, allowing foreign ownership up to the 100% ceiling. In plain terms, a PMA structure may be fully foreign owned nationally for this activity; the record does not set a lower national equity cap. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a founder assessing the national position alone, this is an open category at the stated ownership percentage.

Bali is a conditional, rather than blanket, answer. The record does not mark the activity as categorically blocked for PMA there—its Bali blocked flag is false—but its Bali status depends on scope. The province’s permanent island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for low and medium-low risk KBLI. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others. The Bali PMA route is described as registrable only by declaring the higher-risk scope, and the exact activity must be verified live in OSS. National openness at 100% should therefore not be mistaken for an automatic Bali registration outcome: in Bali, the declared scope’s OSS risk remains decisive.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, 100% foreign ownership is open; in Bali, registration still turns on the declared scope’s OSS risk.
